read.sections.0.heading.back: No one can do everything alone

read.sections.0.text.source: No person can make everything they use. Think about a simple notebook. One person made the paper, another carried the notebooks to a market and another sold them. The things people exchange are goods and services. A good is a thing you can touch and use, such as rice or a pencil. A service is something useful that a person does for someone else, such as teaching, fixing a bicycle or cutting hair. A producer is a person or group that makes a good or provides a service. A consumer is a person who uses or buys it. At Lakeside Market, Ana is a producer when she sells tomatoes. She is also a consumer when she buys rice.
read.sections.0.text.back: No one can make everything they use by themselves. Think of an ordinary notebook. One person makes the paper, another carries the notebooks to market, and another sells them. What people exchange are goods and services. Goods are things you can touch and use, such as rice or a pencil. A service is useful work one person does for another, such as teaching, fixing a bicycle or cutting hair. A producer is a person or group that makes goods or provides services. A consumer is a person who uses or buys those goods or services. At Lakeside market, Ana is a producer when she sells tomatoes, and she is also a consumer when she buys rice.
read.sections.0.text.note: good / service / producer / consumer are สินค้า / บริการ / ผู้บริโภค / ผู้ผลิต (KEY_TERMS). 'ที่ตลาด Lakeside นั้น Ana ...': นั้น was added so two Latin words do not sit side by side; check it reads naturally.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: No one can make everything they use. Think of a notebook. Many people help to make it and sell it. People swap goods and services. A good is a thing you can touch, like rice. A service is work a person does for you, like teaching. A producer makes a good or does a service. A consumer uses or buys it. Ana grows tomatoes, so she is a producer. When she buys rice, she is a consumer.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: No one can make everything they use. Think of a notebook. Many people help make and sell it. People swap goods and services. Goods are things you can touch, such as rice. A service is work someone does for you, such as teaching. Producers make goods or provide services. Consumers use or buy. Ana grows tomatoes, so she is a producer. When she buys rice, she is a consumer.

read.sections.1.text.source: Sometimes people swap goods or services without using money. This is called barter. At Lakeside Market, Kofi swaps some of his bread for some of Sara's eggs. Ravi fixes Nadia's bicycle, and in return Nadia helps Ravi's sister with reading. Barter still happens in many places today. However, it has a problem: both people must want what the other person has, at the same time. Leo has fish and wants rice, but the rice seller does not want fish. Money solves this problem. Leo can sell his fish and use the money to buy rice. Money also helps people compare prices and keep value for later.
read.sections.1.text.back: Sometimes people exchange goods or services without using money. This is called barter. At Lakeside market, Kofi swaps some of his bread for some of Sara's eggs. Ravi fixes Nadia's bicycle, and in return Nadia helps Ravi's younger sister practise reading. Barter still happens in many places today. But barter has one problem: both people must want what the other has at the same time. Leo has fish and wants rice, but the rice seller doesn't want fish. Money can solve this problem. Leo can sell his fish and use the money to buy rice. Money also helps people compare prices and store value to use later.
read.sections.1.text.note: Second pass: "Money solves this problem" was softened to "money helps solve"; now เงินแก้ปัญหานี้ได้. The simpler text keeps เงินช่วยได้ตรงนี้ ("Money helps here"), as the English does.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Sometimes people swap things with no money. This is called barter. Kofi gives Sara bread, and she gives him eggs. Ravi fixes a bike, and Nadia helps his sister read. But barter has a problem. Both people must want what the other has. Leo has fish. He wants rice. The rice seller does not want fish. Money helps here. Leo can sell his fish for money. Then he can buy rice.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Sometimes people swap things without using money. This is called barter. For example, Kofi gives bread to Sara and Sara gives eggs to him. Ravi fixes a bicycle, and Nadia helps his younger sister practise reading. But barter has a problem. Both people must want what the other has. Leo has fish. He wants rice. The rice seller doesn't want fish. Money helps here. Leo can sell the fish for money, and then he can buy rice.
read.sections.1.simpler.note: เช่น and ส่วน were added before Kofi and Ravi so the sentences divide clearly (a Latin name after a space does not end a Thai sentence for the checker or for the eye).

read.sections.2.text.source: Every exchange depends on trust. A buyer trusts that the food is fresh and the scales are fair. A seller trusts that the payment is real. People also trust each other to keep promises, like Nadia's promise to help with reading. If people cheat, others stop trusting them, and trade becomes harder for everyone. This is one reason many markets have rules about fair weights and measures. For thousands of years, markets have brought people together to trade. When people trade fairly, they meet more of their needs, and communities become more connected.
read.sections.2.text.back: Every exchange depends on trust. Buyers trust that the food is fresh and the scales are accurate. Sellers trust that the money they receive is real. People also trust each other to keep promises, like Nadia's promise to help with reading practice. If someone cheats, others stop trusting them, and trade becomes harder for everyone. This is one reason many markets have rules about fair weighing and measuring. Markets have brought people together to trade for thousands of years. When people trade fairly, they get more of what they need, and communities become more connected.
read.sections.2.text.note: 'fair weights and measures' is การชั่งตวงวัดที่ยุติธรรม; 'the scales are fair' is ตาชั่งเที่ยงตรง. Check these market words.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Trade needs trust. A buyer trusts that the food is fresh. A seller trusts that the money is real. People trust each other to keep a promise. If someone cheats, people stop trusting them. Then trade gets harder for everyone. Markets have brought people together for a very long time. When people trade fairly, they get more of what they need.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Trade depends on trust. Buyers trust that the food is fresh. Sellers trust that the money is real. People trust each other to keep promises. If someone cheats, others stop trusting them. Then trade gets harder for everyone. Markets have brought people together for a very long time. When people trade fairly, they get more of what they need.

write.example.source: In this exchange, Ravi gives Nadia a service. He fixes her bicycle. In return, Ravi's little sister gets help with reading from Nadia for one week. This exchange is barter because they swap skills and no money is used. Trust helps because Ravi fixes the bicycle first. He trusts Nadia to keep her promise later. Without trust, Ravi might not help at all, and both of them would lose something useful.
write.example.back: In this exchange, Ravi gives a service to Nadia: he fixes her bicycle. In return, Ravi's younger sister gets help with reading practice from Nadia for one week. This exchange is barter, because they swap skills and don't use money. Trust helps because Ravi fixes the bicycle first. He trusts that Nadia will keep her promise later. Without trust, Ravi might not help at all, and both people would lose something useful.

watch.summary.source: This short video for younger learners explains goods and services. First, it reminds you about needs and wants. Needs are things you must have to live, like food, water and a place to live. Wants are things you would like, like toys and games. People use money to get goods and services. Goods are things people make or grow to sell, like food, books and toys. Services are work people do for others. A doctor helps people stay healthy. A pilot flies a plane. A chef cooks food. Then the video gives some puzzles. A book is a good, but a librarian gives a service when they help you find one. A pizza is a good, but bringing it to your home is a service.
watch.summary.back: This short video was made for younger learners and explains goods and services. First, it reviews needs and wants. Needs are what you must have to live, such as food, water and shelter. Wants are things you would like to have, such as toys and games. People use money to get goods and services. Goods are things people make or grow to sell, such as food, books and toys. Services are work people do for others: doctors help people stay healthy, pilots fly planes, chefs cook food. Then the video gives a puzzle to think about: a book is a good, but a librarian gives a service when helping you find a book. A pizza is a good, but bringing the pizza to your home is a service.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Many learners cannot work legally. Do not ask learners how they or their households earn money. The lesson focuses on swapping and buying everyday things.

educatorNotes.0.source: The market, the food swap and the skill swap are general on purpose. A partner can rename Lakeside Market after a local market, use local foods and goods, and add skill swaps that learners see around them, such as help with repairs, sewing or translation.
educatorNotes.0.back: The market, food swaps and skill swaps in the lesson are general examples on purpose. Partner organisations can rename Lakeside market to a local market, use local foods and goods, and add skill swaps learners see around them, such as helping repair things, sewing or translating.

educatorNotes.1.source: The lesson does not say that barter always came before money. Many historians and anthropologists question the idea that whole communities once lived only by barter; gifts and credit were also common. Barter is shown as one way to exchange that still happens today.
educatorNotes.1.back: The lesson doesn't say barter always came before money. Many historians and anthropologists question the idea that whole communities once lived by barter alone. Gift-giving and credit were also common. The lesson shows barter as one way of exchange that still happens today.
educatorNotes.1.note: 'credit' (in 'gifts and credit') is การให้เชื่อ (buying now, paying later). Check it is not read as 'belief'.

educatorNotes.2.source: The video was made for younger primary learners (grades 3–6). Older learners may find it young in style; the written summary covers the same ideas.
